transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I just can’t seem to sit still anymore, or maybe I never was very good at it, but this past year especially I’m always up doing something. Puttering around the house, fixing little things, rearranging drawers, saying yes to volunteer things when I probably should just stay home.

Even at my age—87, if you can believe it—I feel like I ought to be able to sit with a cup of tea and relax, but then I see a picture frame crooked or remember something in the closet, and up I go. My daughter says, “Mother, just sit down,” but sitting still feels harder than it should.

Over this past year, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually high, euphoric, or irritable along with this restlessness, or does it feel more like you're anxious or worried when you can't sit still?

I don’t know that I’d call it euphoric, no. High mood… that sounds rather grand, doesn’t it? Like someone winning the lottery or dancing in the kitchen. I do get irritated sometimes when people tell me to sit down, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.

It’s more just… I feel like I ought to be doing something, and then I’m up before I’ve even thought it through. Though I do worry too, I suppose, but not always. Sometimes I’m just restless, and then I notice the mail pile, or the plant needs water—well, the fern in the front room is always drooping—and then I’m off doing that.
Have you started or changed any medications recently, especially any new prescriptions from your doctor in the past few months?

I’m not sure, honestly. I don’t think anything major has changed, but I’d have to look at the little bottles—my daughter lines them up for me sometimes, and then I move them because I don’t like them cluttering the counter, which defeats the purpose, I suppose.

No new prescription comes to mind right this minute. My regular doctor did mention something at the last visit, but now I’m mixing that up with the flu shot appointment, so… I don’t want to say wrong. I’d need to check.

When you feel this urge to get up and move, do you ever notice it specifically in your legs—like an uncomfortable, crawling, or achy feeling that makes you want to move them, especially in the evening or when you're lying down at night?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed anything like crawling, no… not that I can put my finger on. My legs get tired sometimes, but at 87 I suppose everyone’s legs have opinions.

At night, I’m more likely to remember I left something in the kitchen or think, “Did I lock the back door?”—though half the time I have—and then I’m up checking. But a creepy feeling in my legs specifically? I don’t think so.
Have you noticed any unexpected weight loss, feeling unusually warm or sweaty, or your heart racing over this past year?

I haven’t really noticed anything like that, no. My weight… well, I don’t keep track as closely as I probably should. The scale is in the bathroom, but it’s behind a basket of towels, and then I forget it’s there.

Feeling warm or sweaty—only if the room is too warm, I suppose. My daughter is always telling me I keep the house like a greenhouse. And my heart racing… I don’t think so. Nothing that made me stop and think, “Oh, that’s odd.”

Have you or your family noticed any recent changes in your memory, like forgetting recent conversations, repeating questions, or having trouble keeping track of dates or tasks you used to handle easily?

I’m not sure… I mean, I do forget things, but I’ve always been a bit that way. My daughter says I’ll put the mail down and then ask where it went, but honestly, who can keep track when there are three piles on the table and one of them is coupons from last month?

Dates, I use the calendar on the fridge—when I remember to look at it. I don’t know that it’s a new change, though. I don’t think we’ve had any big alarming thing, not that anyone’s sat me down about it.
Has your daughter or anyone else had to start helping you with things you used to handle on your own, like paying bills, managing your medications, or keeping track of appointments?

I don’t think there’s been any sort of big change like that… at least not that I’m aware of. My daughter does ask me about things, but daughters do that, don’t they? Mine has always been one to hover a bit—she’ll come in and notice a stack of envelopes and suddenly it’s a whole production.

But no, I can’t say someone has had to take over anything. I may be a little scattered with keeping things in one place, but I don’t think there’s been a new arrangement or anything formal like that.
Would you say you spend a lot of time worrying about several different things—like your health, family, or household tasks—and that this worry feels hard to switch off or control?

I don’t know that I’d call it worrying a lot. I mean, I think about things—everybody does, don’t they? The house, whether I remembered to do something, my daughter fussing about this or that.

But it’s not like I sit there all day fretting, I don’t think. Sometimes I’ll start thinking about one thing and then notice the curtains need washing, and then I’m in the closet looking for something completely different. So… hard to say, really.
Have you ever found yourself confused about where you are, what day it is, or gotten lost or disoriented in places that used to be familiar to you, like your own neighborhood?

I don’t think so… not like lost-lost. I mean, sometimes I’ll walk into a room and think, “Now why did I come in here?” but that’s not the same thing, is it?

In the neighborhood, I know where I am. Though they did change that corner store sign a while back—or maybe it just feels new because everything’s so bright now—and for a second I’ll think, “Was that always there?” But no, I haven’t found myself somewhere and not known where I was. As for the day, I check the paper or the calendar if I need to.
Would it be alright if I asked you a few quick questions to check your memory and concentration right now—like today's date or repeating a short list of words back to me?

Oh—yes, I suppose that would be alright. I’m not always fond of little tests, they make me feel like I’m back in school and I never did like being put on the spot. I remember one professor I had who would call on you without warning—awful habit.

But yes, go ahead. Just tell me what you want me to do, and I’ll try.
Can you tell me today's full date, including the day of the week, month, day, and year?

Oh, the full date… let me think. I should know that, I looked at the calendar this morning—or was that yesterday? I keep one by the phone, but then my daughter moved some papers around and I hate when things aren’t where I expect them.

It’s… I’m not sure of the exact full date right this second. I could tell you if I checked the calendar. The day of the week slips out of my head unless I’ve got an appointment or the trash has to go out.
I’m going to say three words—apple, table, and coin. Can you repeat them back to me now, and then I’ll ask you to recall them again in a few minutes?
Apple, table, and coin. Apple… table… coin. I’ll try to hold onto them—though now I’m picturing an apple sitting on my kitchen table, which maybe helps, I don’t know.
Now, can you tell me the three words I asked you to remember a few minutes ago?

Oh dear… it was three little things, wasn’t it? I remember the apple, because I made that picture in my head on the kitchen table. And there was… was it a coin? I’m pretty sure coin was one.

The middle one is slipping away from me now. Something in the kitchen? No, wait—table, yes, table. Apple, table, coin. I think that was it.
Has your daughter or anyone mentioned any time when forgetting something led to a real problem—like missing an important appointment, taking your medication incorrectly, or leaving the stove on?

I’m not sure, honestly. My daughter will say things like, “Mom, you forgot again,” but I can’t think of a big serious problem from it right now.

I mean, I write things down, though then the little notes end up under the mail—my kitchen counter gets like a landing strip, you know, everything comes in there. But as far as missing something truly important or, well, causing trouble… I don’t know. Nothing is coming to mind unless she’s remembering something I’m not.

Have you been diagnosed with any medical conditions recently, or had any illnesses, infections, head injuries, or hospital stays this past year that your doctor mentioned might affect your brain or thinking?

Hmm… not that I can think of. I mean, I’ve had the usual doctor visits, and at my age there’s always someone wanting to check something, you know how it is. But nobody has sat me down and said, “This could affect your thinking,” or anything like that.

No hospital stay or head bump that I remember. Infections… I don’t think so. I’d have to ask my daughter if there was something she remembers, because she keeps track of things better than I do sometimes.
Right now, can you still manage things like cooking your own meals, handling your finances, and taking your medications entirely on your own without any help or reminders from your daughter?

Well… I think so, mostly. I make myself something to eat, nothing fancy—though I used to make a wonderful pot roast, my husband loved that, and now it feels silly cooking a big thing for one person.

Finances… my daughter looks in on things sometimes, I think, but I can’t tell you exactly how much. The pills, I have my little setup for them. I don’t know if you’d call that “entirely on my own,” because she does remind me here and there. I suppose I’d have to ask her to be sure.
Over this past year, would you say your memory and your ability to manage daily tasks have been gradually getting worse, or have they stayed pretty much the same the whole time?

I’m not sure I could say it’s been getting worse, exactly. It feels… about the same to me, I guess, but then again days run together a bit when you’re not working anymore. Mondays don’t feel like Mondays, you know?

My daughter might notice things more than I do. I still do my usual things, or I think I do. Some days I’m more scattered, but I don’t know if that’s worse or just… how things are. I’d have to think on it.
Has your daughter had to take over any tasks completely—like paying the bills or managing your medications—because you were no longer able to do them safely on your own?

I don’t think she’s taken over completely, no… at least not that I know of. She does help me keep an eye on things, but “taken over” sounds so official, doesn’t it?

The bills—I used to sit with my checkbook at the kitchen table, and my husband would always say I made it into a whole production with tea and everything. These days some of it is online, which I don’t like much. My daughter understands all that better than I do.

With the pills, I have my little system, though she’ll ask me, “Did you take them?” now and then. But I wouldn’t say she’s fully doing it for me. I’d have to ask her exactly how much she thinks she’s doing, because she might say it differently.

Thinking back to a year ago, is there any specific task—like paying a bill, cooking a meal, or managing your pills—that you used to do completely on your own but now truly cannot do without your daughter's help?

I can’t think of one, not a specific one like that. I mean, I still make food for myself—though I’m not making big dinners, but I stopped doing that after my husband passed, really. It’s funny, I still have some of his old recipe cards in the drawer, though he never cooked a day in his life.

The bills and pills… I don’t know. My daughter helps, or reminds me, but I wouldn’t say there’s one thing I truly cannot do anymore. At least, nothing comes to mind right now. Maybe she’d have a better answer than I would.
Would it be alright if I spoke briefly with your daughter, either now or by phone, to get her perspective on how you're managing day-to-day tasks like bills and medications?

Yes, I suppose that would be alright. She’s better at remembering the details anyway—she has that little phone with everything in it, calendar and reminders and all that. I still like a paper calendar myself, though mine gets covered in notes and then I can’t tell which note was for what.

But yes, you can talk to her. If she’s available now, fine, or you could call her. I don’t mind, as long as she knows you’re calling and doesn’t think it’s one of those nuisance calls. She gets so many of those.

doctor.intent: Establish the primary reason for the visit
doctor.question: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in today?

target_item.name: Constant_Activity
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that for the past year or so I feel like I’m always puttering, fixing, arranging, or volunteering for one more thing, and even at 87 I have a hard time just sitting down and being still.
target_item.reason: This is the first reply of the consultation, so I am returning the chief complaint symptom code S014.

patient.answer:
Well, I suppose what brings me in is… I just can’t seem to sit still anymore, or maybe I never was very good at it, but this past year especially I’m always up doing something. Puttering around the house, fixing little things, rearranging drawers, saying yes to volunteer things when I probably should just stay home.

Even at my age—87, if you can believe it—I feel like I ought to be able to sit with a cup of tea and relax, but then I see a picture frame crooked or remember something in the closet, and up I go. My daughter says, “Mother, just sit down,” but sitting still feels harder than it should.

inference.note: Initial differential based on chronic restlessness/inability to sit still in an elderly patient: generalized anxiety, hypomania/mania, adult ADHD, hyperthyroidism, medication-induced akathisia, and early dementia with behavioral agitation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the restlessness is accompanied by an elevated, euphoric, or unusually irritable mood (suggesting mania) versus anxious worry, to help distinguish bipolar/mania from anxiety-related causes.
doctor.question: Over this past year, have you noticed your mood feeling unusually high, euphoric, or irritable along with this restlessness, or does it feel more like you're anxious or worried when you can't sit still?

target_item.reason: The question is asking about whether the restlessness is accompanied by elevated/irritable mood or anxiety/worry, but the symptom profile does not include mood or anxiety symptoms.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I’d call it euphoric, no. High mood… that sounds rather grand, doesn’t it? Like someone winning the lottery or dancing in the kitchen. I do get irritated sometimes when people tell me to sit down, but I’m not sure if that’s what you mean.

It’s more just… I feel like I ought to be doing something, and then I’m up before I’ve even thought it through. Though I do worry too, I suppose, but not always. Sometimes I’m just restless, and then I notice the mail pile, or the plant needs water—well, the fern in the front room is always drooping—and then I’m off doing that.
